content_units: Budget Snapshot for a $4,200 Take-Home Pay
You bring in   $4,200/month  . Your fixed monthly costs total   $2,790  , leaving   $1,410/month   before choosing Plan A or Plan B.
To estimate your emergency-fund goal, I’m using your listed fixed costs as the base monthly essential spending.
Plan A vs Plan B Cash Flow
Plan   Emergency Fund   Extra Debt Payment   Total Planned Saving/Debt Push   Monthly Left Over After Plan   Months to 3-Month Cushion
\ 3-month emergency cushion target based on essentials:   $2,790 × 3 = $8,370
Option 1:   Plan A     Builds cash reserves faster while still paying debt above minimum   Best fit for stress reduction
- Reaches your emergency cushion much faster
- More cash on hand lowers stress from surprise expenses
- Reduces chance of needing new debt when something goes wrong
- Still makes meaningful extra debt progress
- Slower debt payoff than Plan B
- You may pay more interest over time if your debt rate is high
Option 2:   Plan B     Pays debt down more aggressively but builds cash slowly   Better only if debt interest is the urgent issue
- Can improve monthly flexibility sooner once debt is gone
- Higher risk of financial stress if an unexpected bill hits
- More likely to rely on credit again before the cushion is ready
Best fit for your stated priorities
Because your top priorities are   reducing financial stress   and   building a 3-month emergency cushion  ,   Plan A is the better choice  .
- Your priority order favors   cash safety first
- Plan A gets you to the 3-month cushion in about   14 months  , versus about   28 months   with Plan B
- Both plans leave the same monthly leftover cash, so the real difference is   where the $900 goes
- Having stronger reserves usually feels better day-to-day than accelerating debt slightly more
- Keep the extra   $510/month   as flexible buffer for irregular expenses or small sinking funds
- Once your emergency fund reaches at least   1–3 months  , consider shifting more toward debt payoff
- After hitting   $8,370  , redirect the $600 emergency contribution toward debt
